q: Which of these is NOT a condition for claiming ITC under section 16(2)?
options: You have a tax invoice or debit note
You've received the goods or services
The supplier has paid the tax to the government
The supplier is registered in the same state as you
exp: Inter-state purchases with IGST are fully creditable. The conditions are: document, receipt, tax actually paid, return filed, and the invoice appears in GSTR-2B.

q: Under section 16(2)(aa), ITC is available only if:
options: The invoice is uploaded in your purchase register
The supplier has reported the invoice in GSTR-1/IFF and it's communicated to you (in GSTR-2B)
The payment is made by cheque
exp: Since 1 January 2022, ITC is restricted to invoices reflected in GSTR-2B.

q: Goods ordered in one invoice arrive in three lots over three months. When can ITC be claimed?
options: On receipt of the last lot
exp: Proviso to s.16(2)(b).

q: You paid your supplier 200 days after the invoice date. What happens to ITC already claimed?
options: It must be reversed (added to output liability) with interest, and can be re-claimed when you pay
exp: If the value plus tax isn't paid within 180 days of the invoice, ITC is reversed with interest and can be re-availed on payment.
ref: CGST Act, s.16(2) second proviso; r.37

q: Under bill-to ship-to, the person to whom the goods are billed is deemed to have received them, even though they went to a third party.
exp: Explanation to s.16(2)(b), so the billed buyer can claim ITC.

q: You claimed depreciation under income tax on the full cost of a machine, including the GST. Can you also claim ITC on it?
options: No, if depreciation is claimed on the tax component, ITC isn't allowed
exp: Section 16(3) prevents a double benefit.

q: ITC on capital goods is available in full in the year of purchase, not spread over years.
exp: Unlike the old CENVAT 50:50 split, GST allows full ITC on capital goods upfront, subject to the other conditions.

q: What's the last date to claim ITC for an invoice dated 15 February 2025 (FY 2024-25)?
options: 30 November 2025, or the date you file the annual return, whichever is earlier
exp: Section 16(4): 30 November following the end of the financial year, or the annual return date if earlier.

q: For a debit note issued in May 2025 for a supply invoiced in January 2025, the ITC time limit is determined by:
options: The financial year of the debit note date
exp: The Finance Act 2021 delinked the debit note from the underlying invoice for the section 16(4) time limit.

q: ITC on a car (5-seater) bought for the director's official use is:
exp: Motor vehicles for transport of persons with seating capacity up to 13 (including driver) are blocked, unless used for further supply of vehicles, passenger transport or driving training.

q: A car dealer buys cars for resale. ITC?
options: Available, since it's for further supply of such vehicles
exp: The exception in s.17(5)(a) covers further supply of vehicles.

q: A trucking company buys a truck to carry goods. ITC?
options: Available, blocked credit applies only to vehicles for transporting persons
exp: Vehicles for transporting goods aren't in the blocked list.

q: ITC on food and beverages served to employees at an office party is:
options: Blocked, unless providing it is mandatory under a law or the recipient uses it for the same category of outward supply
exp: Section 17(5)(b)(i). A caterer buying food services for catering can claim it; an IT company throwing a party can't.

q: A company constructs its own office building. ITC on cement and steel is:
options: Available as they're used in business
Blocked, goods and services for construction of immovable property on own account (other than plant and machinery) are blocked
Available only if the building is rented out later
exp: Section 17(5)(d). The Supreme Court in Safari Retreats (2024) held a building can qualify as 'plant' under a functionality test; the law was later amended retrospectively to clarify 'plant or machinery'.

q: Which is NOT a blocked credit?
options: Health insurance for employees where not mandated by law
Machinery used to manufacture taxable goods
exp: Machinery for taxable supplies is fine. CSR spends were added to blocked credits from 1 October 2023.

q: Goods are destroyed in a fire at the warehouse. What happens to the ITC taken on them?
options: ITC must be reversed, goods lost, stolen or destroyed are blocked
exp: Section 17(5)(h). This covers goods lost, stolen, destroyed, written off, or disposed of as gifts or free samples.

q: Tax paid under section 74 (demand involving fraud or suppression) is:
exp: Section 17(5)(i) blocks ITC of tax paid under sections 74, 129 and 130. For FY 2024-25 onwards the equivalent is tax paid under s.74A in fraud cases.

q: Works contract services for building a factory shed are blocked, but ITC on plant and machinery installed inside is allowed.
exp: 'Plant and machinery' includes apparatus and equipment fixed to earth by foundation, but excludes land, buildings and civil structures.

q: A business makes both taxable and exempt supplies and has common ITC on rent. What's the treatment?
options: Claim all, then reverse the portion attributable to exempt supplies under rule 42
exp: Section 17(2) with rule 42 for inputs and input services, and rule 43 for capital goods.

q: A bank chooses the option under section 17(4). What does it mean?
options: It claims 50% of eligible ITC every month and the rest lapses, instead of doing rule 42 apportionment
It pays tax on reverse charge
exp: Banks and financial institutions can take 50% of eligible ITC as a simplified option.

q: Where is permanent ITC reversal (like section 17(5) blocked credit) reported in GSTR-3B?
exp: 4(B)(1) is for reversals under rules 38, 42, 43 and s.17(5), which can't be reclaimed. 4(B)(2) is for temporary reversals that may be reclaimed later.

q: In what order must ITC be utilised?
options: IGST credit first (IGST, then CGST and SGST in any order), then CGST and SGST credits
exp: Section 49 and rule 88A: IGST credit must be fully used before CGST or SGST credit. CGST credit can pay CGST then IGST; SGST credit pays SGST then IGST.

q: CGST credit can be used to pay SGST liability.
exp: Never. CGST and SGST go to different governments, so they can't cross-pay. Either can pay IGST.

q: ITC in the electronic credit ledger can be used to pay interest and late fees.
exp: Credit ledger can only pay output tax. Interest, penalty and fees must be paid through the cash ledger.

q: Rule 86B restricts use of credit ledger to 99% of output tax. Which taxpayer does it apply to?
options: Those with taxable supplies (other than exempt and zero-rated) above ₹50 lakh in a month, unless an exception applies
exp: Such taxpayers must pay at least 1% of output tax in cash, unless exceptions apply (e.g. more than ₹1 lakh income tax paid in each of the last two years, or refunds above ₹1 lakh).

q: Under rule 86A, an officer can block the electronic credit ledger if ITC is suspected to be fraudulent. For how long?
exp: The restriction lapses after one year from the date it's imposed.

q: From 1 April 2025, a company whose head office receives common input services (like audit fees) for branches in several states must:
options: Claim it all at the head office
Register as an Input Service Distributor and distribute the credit
Claim at the branch with the largest turnover
exp: The Finance Act 2024 made ISD registration mandatory for distributing common input service credit, including RCM services.

q: How does an ISD distribute credit to its units?
options: Through an ISD invoice, reported in GSTR-6
exp: ISD files GSTR-6 monthly; recipients see it in GSTR-2B.

q: A dealer gets newly registered and applies within 30 days of becoming liable. What about ITC on opening stock?
options: Available on inputs in stock, semi-finished and finished goods on the day before liability arose
exp: Section 18(1)(a), claimed via ITC-01 within 30 days.

q: A company bought a machine two years ago for ₹10 lakh plus ₹1.8 lakh GST (ITC claimed). It now sells the machine for ₹4 lakh. How much GST must it pay on the sale?
model: Under section 18(6), for capital goods on which ITC was taken, the tax payable on transfer is the higher of: (a) ITC taken reduced by 5 percentage points per quarter of use, or (b) tax on the transaction value. Two years is 8 quarters, so ITC minus 40%: ₹1.8 lakh x 60% = ₹1.08 lakh. Tax on transaction value at 18% is ₹72,000. The company pays the higher, ₹1.08 lakh.
points: Higher of adjusted ITC or tax on transaction value
exp: This stops businesses from buying capital goods with full ITC and selling them cheap soon after.

q: A client (IT company) asks if it can claim ITC on a ₹2 lakh bill for an employee offsite at a resort (rooms and food). The CA says:
options: Food and beverages are blocked; accommodation for business purpose may be eligible if the place of supply matches the client's registered state
All claimable if paid by card
exp: Section 17(5)(b) blocks food and beverages and outdoor catering. Hotel stay for business isn't in the blocked list, but POS rules often make it unusable.

q: A client paid a supplier in full and has the invoice, but the supplier never deposited the GST. The department asks the client to reverse ITC. Is that possible under the law?
options: No, the client paid in good faith
Yes, section 16(2)(c) requires tax to be actually paid to the government; courts are divided on bona fide buyers, but the department can pursue it
exp: The Supreme Court upheld recovery from buyers in some contexts, while several High Courts protected genuine buyers where the department didn't first pursue the supplier. It's a live litigation area.

q: On 5 December 2025, a client finds FY 2024-25 invoices worth ₹3 lakh ITC never claimed. What's the position?
options: The section 16(4) deadline (30 November 2025) has passed, so the ITC is lost
exp: This is why CAs run an ITC sweep in October and November.
